tasks.name: Decompose recursive tree problems and return useful subtree state
Choose traversal order and exploit tree ordering
Represent and query shared string prefixes with tries

concepts.name: Recursive base case and progress
concepts.description: Define when recursion stops and ensure every recursive call moves to a strictly smaller or simpler subproblem.

concepts.name: Recursive decompose/combine
concepts.description: Express a hierarchical problem as the same problem on child substructures, then combine child results into the parent result.

concepts.name: Tree DFS return state
concepts.description: Choose the smallest value each subtree must return so the parent can compute its own answer.

concepts.name: Tree traversal order
concepts.description: Choose preorder, inorder, or postorder according to whether parent work happens before, between, or after child work.

concepts.name: Tree breadth-first levels
concepts.description: Use a FIFO frontier to visit tree nodes by depth and preserve level boundaries when the output is distance-from-root based.

concepts.name: Binary-search-tree ordered search
concepts.description: Use the BST ordering invariant to choose one child subtree and discard the other during key search or ordered queries.

concepts.name: Trie prefix path
concepts.description: Represent string keys character by character so shared prefixes reuse the same path and prefix queries stop at the prefix node.

concepts.name: Trie terminal marker
concepts.description: Distinguish a complete stored key from a prefix path by recording whether a trie node terminates a key.

concepts.name: Trie prefix query
concepts.description: Use the node reached by a prefix as the frontier for autocomplete, prefix enumeration, or longest-prefix style lookups.

questions.prompt: A binary tree is represented as `[value, left, right]`, with `None` for an empty child. Implement `tree_height(tree)`: empty height is 0 and a leaf has height 1.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: An empty subtree returns 0. A non-empty subtree returns one plus the larger child height.
hints: The recursive calls must use the left and right child subtrees.
Return only the state the parent needs: subtree height.

questions.prompt: Repair `count_nodes`. The recursive call on `tree` itself never makes structural progress.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: Every recursive call must move to a smaller subtree. Recurse on `left` and `right`, not on the current tree again.
hints: A recursive argument should be structurally smaller.
The two child variables are already available.

questions.prompt: Implement `tree_sum(tree)` for `[value, left, right]` trees. Return the sum of every node value. Empty trees sum to 0.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: The parent answer is local value plus the two child-subtree sums.
hints: Use 0 as the empty-subtree identity.
Combine left sum, right sum, and the current value.

error_codes.description: One or more behavioral tests did not pass.

questions.prompt: Implement `count_leaves(tree)`. A leaf is a non-empty node with BOTH children `None`. Return the number of leaves.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: The base cases distinguish empty trees from leaves. Internal nodes combine leaf counts from child subtrees.
hints: Check the leaf condition before recursing further.
An empty child is not a leaf.

error_codes.description: One or more behavioral tests did not pass.

questions.prompt: Implement `is_height_balanced(tree)`. A tree is height-balanced when, at EVERY node, left and right subtree heights differ by at most 1. Target O(n) time.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: A single DFS can return subtree height when balanced and a failure sentinel when unbalanced, avoiding repeated height recomputation.
hints: The parent needs both height and whether a child already failed.
A sentinel such as `-1` can encode failure.

error_codes.description: One or more behavioral tests did not pass.

questions.prompt: Implement `tree_diameter_edges(tree)`. Return the maximum number of EDGES on any path between two nodes. The path may or may not pass through the root. Empty and single-node trees have diameter 0. Target O(n).
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: Each subtree should return height while the traversal also tracks the best `left_height + right_height` path found so far.
hints: Do not recompute subtree heights from scratch.
At each node, the path through that node uses both child heights.

error_codes.description: One or more behavioral tests did not pass.

questions.prompt: Implement `max_root_to_leaf_sum(tree)`. The tree is non-empty. Return the maximum sum along a path from the root to any LEAF. Node values may be negative.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: A missing child is not an alternative zero-value path; the path must end at a real leaf. Handle one-child nodes carefully.
hints: A leaf returns its own value.
If only one child exists, the path must continue through that child.

questions.prompt: Complete `tree_height(tree)`. A binary tree is represented as `[value, left, right]`, and `None` means an empty child. Height is measured in NODES. Example: an empty tree has height 0, a leaf such as `[7, None, None]` has height 1, and `[1, [2, None, None], None]` has height 2. The parent height is one level above its taller child. Fill the empty-tree base case and the expression that combines the two child heights.
questions.explanation: Empty height is 0; a node contributes one level above the taller child.
hints: The empty subtree contributes no node to a root-to-leaf path.
A non-empty node contributes one plus the taller child height.

error_codes.description: One or more code blanks are incorrect.

questions.prompt: Implement `preorder_values(tree)` for `[value, left, right]` trees. Return values in root, left, right order.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: Preorder processes the current node before either child subtree.
hints: For an empty tree return an empty list.
Combine `[value] + preorder(left) + preorder(right)` or equivalent.

error_codes.description: One or more behavioral tests did not pass.

questions.prompt: Implement `postorder_values(tree)`. Return values in left, right, root order.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: Postorder waits until both child subtrees are processed before the parent.
hints: Process left and right before appending the current value.
This order is useful when parent work depends on completed children.

error_codes.description: One or more behavioral tests did not pass.

questions.prompt: Implement `level_order(tree)`. Return node values in breadth-first order from shallowest level to deepest, left to right within each level.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: A FIFO queue visits all nodes at one depth before later depths.
hints: Enqueue the root if it exists.
When a node is removed, enqueue each non-empty child.

error_codes.description: One or more behavioral tests did not pass.

questions.prompt: Implement `bst_contains(tree, target)`. The tree is a valid BST with distinct values. Return whether `target` exists without traversing both subtrees.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: BST ordering lets each comparison discard one whole subtree: smaller targets go left and larger targets go right.
hints: Do not recursively search both children.
Compare target with the current node value.

error_codes.description: One or more behavioral tests did not pass.

questions.prompt: Implement `is_valid_bst(tree)`. Values must be STRICTLY ordered: every value in a left subtree is smaller than its ancestor and every value in a right subtree is larger. Duplicate values are invalid.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: Checking only parent/child comparisons is insufficient. Carry the allowable `(low, high)` range inherited from every ancestor.
hints: Left recursion tightens the upper bound to the current value.
Right recursion tightens the lower bound.

error_codes.description: One or more behavioral tests did not pass.

questions.prompt: Implement `kth_smallest_bst(tree, k)` for a valid BST with distinct values. `k` is 1-based and valid. Return the kth smallest value.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: Inorder traversal of a BST yields ascending values. Count visited nodes in inorder order until reaching k.
hints: Traversal order is left, root, right.
You may use an iterative stack or recursive counter.

error_codes.description: One or more behavioral tests did not pass.

questions.prompt: Implement `lowest_common_ancestor_bst(tree, a, b)`. The tree is a valid BST with distinct values, and both values exist. Return the value of their lowest common ancestor.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: If both targets are smaller, move left; if both are larger, move right. Otherwise the current node is where their search paths split or one target equals the current node.
hints: Normalize with `lo=min(a,b)` and `hi=max(a,b)` if useful.
The first node with `lo <= value <= hi` is the answer.

questions.prompt: Complete `level_order(tree)`. A binary tree is `[value, left, right]` with `None` for empty children. Return node values in breadth-first order: shallowest level first, left to right within a level. Example: `[1, [2, [4,None,None], None], [3,None,None]] -> [1, 2, 3, 4]`. `queue` is a `deque` and must behave FIFO: remove the OLDEST discovered node from the front, then append each non-empty child to the back. Fill those three queue operations.
questions.explanation: BFS removes the oldest discovered node and appends newly discovered children to the back.
hints: FIFO processing removes from the left side of a deque.
Discovered children are appended to the back so earlier discoveries are processed first.

questions.prompt: Implement `trie_contains(words, key)`. Build a trie from `words`, then return `True` only if `key` is stored as a COMPLETE word. A key that is only a prefix of a longer stored word must return `False`.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: Walk one child per character. Reaching the final path is not enough; the final node must also have its terminal marker set.
hints: Return false immediately if a character edge is missing.
After the walk, return `node.terminal`.

questions.prompt: Implement `trie_has_prefix(words, prefix)`. Return whether at least one stored word begins with `prefix`. The prefix itself does NOT need to be a complete word.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: A prefix query only needs the path to exist. It does not require a terminal marker at the final prefix node.
hints: Walk the prefix characters from the root.
If every edge exists, the prefix exists.

questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: Path existence answers a prefix query. Exact membership additionally requires the final node's terminal marker.

questions.prompt: Implement `autocomplete(words, prefix)`. Build a trie, walk to the prefix node, then return every stored word beginning with `prefix` in lexicographic order.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: First walk only the prefix. Then DFS from that node; a terminal node emits the accumulated characters as one complete word.
hints: Sort child characters during DFS for lexicographic output.
If the prefix path is missing, return an empty list.

questions.prompt: Implement `longest_stored_prefix(words, query)`. Return the longest COMPLETE stored word that is a prefix of `query`, or `""` if none exists.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: Walk the query from the trie root and remember the deepest position whose node is terminal. Stop when the next character edge is missing.
hints: A traversed path is not automatically a stored key.
Update the best answer only at terminal nodes.

questions.prompt: Implement `count_prefix_queries(words, prefixes)`. Build ONE trie from `words`, storing enough state at each node to answer how many stored words begin with each prefix. Return counts in the same order as `prefixes`.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: Increment a node's prefix count whenever an inserted word passes through that node. Then each query walks only its prefix and reads the stored count.
hints: The root can store the total word count for the empty prefix.
Do not scan all words separately for every query.

questions.prompt: Implement `replace_with_shortest_root(roots, words)`. For each word, if one or more stored roots are prefixes of it, replace the word with the SHORTEST such root. Otherwise keep the word. Return the transformed list.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: Walk each word character by character. The first terminal trie node encountered is the shortest stored root, so the search can stop immediately.
hints: Check `terminal` after every character step.
If the path breaks before a terminal node, keep the original word.

questions.prompt: Complete trie insertion. Each `TrieNode` has a `children` dictionary mapping one character to the next node and a `terminal` flag that is True only when a COMPLETE stored word ends there. Example: to insert `"cat"`, start at the root, follow/create the `c` child, then `a`, then `t`, and finally mark only the node after `t` as terminal. Shared prefixes must reuse existing child nodes instead of replacing them. Fill the child creation, path advance, and final terminal update.
questions.explanation: Each character follows or creates one trie edge. The terminal marker is set only after all characters of the key have been consumed.
hints: Create a new TrieNode only when the current character edge does not already exist.
After processing all characters, mark the node you ended on as a complete key.
